clue.text: Tortoise's protection from speeding vehicle?

parts.note: a car is an everyday vehicle
apace means quickly, at speed

explanation.surface: A tortoise needs a shell to protect it from a car racing along.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives the speed first, but the charade runs CAR then APACE, with 'from' as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard upper shell of a tortoise or turtle is its armour, guarding the soft body inside.

clue.text: Responsibility for attack

explanation.surface: Someone takes on a duty to assault.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in someone's care or keeping, and a headlong rush at an enemy.

clue.text: Cancel, and ring again?

parts.note: re- is the prefix meaning again
a peal is a ringing of bells

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to call off or phone back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is a link; the charade runs RE then PEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: To revoke a law is to withdraw it formally.

clue.text: Gasps at underwear

explanation.surface: Someone breathes hard at the sight of underclothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Breathes hard and fast, and the British word for knickers or underpants.

clue.text: Salad leaves with elegant round lines

parts.note: chic means elegant
O is a round shape
RY is short for railway, a set of lines

explanation.surface: Salad greens arranged in neat rings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lines' gives RY, railway lines, a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: A bitter leaf related to endive, eaten raw in salads.

clue.text: Drunk has problem returning chemistry paper

parts.note: lit is slang for drunk

indicators.note: returning means the word for a problem is read backwards

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem

explanation.surface: A tipsy student with a homework problem hands in a chemistry paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' looks like a noun for the student but is the slang adjective; 'returning' reads the problem backwards, and 'has' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Indicator strips dipped into liquids in the school laboratory change colour to show acid or alkali.

clue.text: Nine trios playing a supplementary piece

indicators.note: playing suggests musicians performing, but here signals the letters being rearranged

explanation.surface: Nine groups of three musicians perform an extra item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' rearranges NINE and TRIOS together.
explanation.definitionFit: Something put into a text or a newspaper, an added leaflet or passage, is an extra inserted item.

clue.text: Wood piles round a corner U L C Y

indicators.note: round means the word for piles goes about the next pieces

parts.note: piles means many, lots
to hog is to corner or monopolise

explanation.surface: Logs heaped about a cornered space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corner' is the verb, to monopolise; 'round' wraps piles about A and that verb. The trailing U L C Y is stray print in the source, not part of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A reddish-brown tropical hardwood prized for furniture.

clue.text: Paste diamond that's lucky A A S T A M for some?

definitions.text: lucky A A S T A M for some?

parts.note: paste is fake jewellery, a sham
rock is slang for a diamond

explanation.surface: A fake diamond brings some people good fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: The three-leaved shamrock is Ireland's emblem, lucky for the Irish; A A S T A M is stray print in the source.
explanation.definitionFit: A clover sprig is an Irish emblem of good fortune.

clue.text: Additional notes to take place, but no introduction, the French figure

indicators.note: losing its introduction means the first letter of the word for take place is dropped

parts.note: to happen is to take place
dix is the French number ten

explanation.surface: A writer adds supplementary notes and a French number, skipping the introduction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but no introduction' removes the H from HAPPEN, leaving APPEN; DIX is French for ten.
explanation.definitionFit: Supplementary material placed at the end of a book or report sits behind the main text.

clue.text: Top mark for maths wangled, bringing complaint

parts.note: A is the top grade in an exam

indicators.note: wangled means fiddled or manipulated, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A pupil fiddles a maths result to an A grade and gets a complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wangled' signals the anagram of the subject; 'for' and 'bringing' are links. 'Complaint' is the medical sense, an ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint can mean an illness, and this is a chronic breathing disorder.

clue.text: Ancient character's whip, we hear

indicators.note: we hear means the word for whip is said aloud

parts.note: a beater whips eggs or cream

explanation.surface: An old figure's lash, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: BEATER and BETA sound alike in non-rhotic British speech. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The second letter of the Greek alphabet is a character from an ancient script.

clue.text: Old bag happy to administer biblical justice

parts.note: glad means happy
stoning was the punishment prescribed in the Bible for some offences

explanation.surface: An old woman seems pleased to dole out punishment by the book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old bag' suggests an unpleasant old woman; it is a type of travelling bag named after the Victorian prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: A hinged leather travelling case named after a Victorian prime minister is an old-fashioned portmanteau.

clue.text: Boy got it

explanation.surface: A lad acknowledges a message.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's first name, and the radio operators' word confirming a message was received and understood.

clue.text: Not to be trusted for the moment, beheaded!

indicators.note: beheaded means the first letter of the word for moment is cut off

parts.note: a jiffy is a moment

explanation.surface: Someone untrustworthy has been beheaded for the time being.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beheaded' drops J from JIFFY; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Dubious or doubtful things are unreliable and invite suspicion.

clue.text: Instrument providing pulse CORPORAL NERVE

explanation.surface: An instrument that keeps a beat.
explanation.definitionFit: A small high-pitched flute, and a pale green bean, a kind of edible legume. CORPORAL NERVE is stray print.

clue.text: County retains one in charge of flying machines

indicators.note: retains means the county holds the next piece inside it

parts.note: Avon was an English county, around Bristol, from 1974 to 1996
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A county keeps one official responsible for its aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retains' signals the container; 'of flying machines' is an adjectival definition, matching an adjective answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective relates to aircraft electronics, aviation equipment and the like.

clue.text: Put off supporting black guard

parts.note: pro means in favour of, supporting
read as one word, a blackguard is a rogue

explanation.surface: A dark-clad sentry delays something he supports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'black guard' splits blackguard, a scoundrel.
explanation.definitionFit: To discontinue a session of parliament without dissolving it is to postpone its business.

clue.text: Expert, so no stupid idiots!

parts.note: a buff is an enthusiast and expert

indicators.note: stupid suggests a dim arrangement, so these letters are muddled

explanation.surface: An expert insists he is no fool, unlike the stupid ones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stupid' rearranges SO and NO into OONS.
explanation.definitionFit: Clowns and fools who act ridiculously are silly people.

clue.text: Fruit waffle

explanation.surface: A fruity pudding and some idle chatter.
explanation.definitionFit: A pink-stalked plant eaten as a fruit, and the word actors mutter to sound like background talk, so meaningless chatter.

clue.text: Fish with deep voice

explanation.surface: A fish with a low singing voice.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea perch, and the lowest male singing voice.

clue.text: A fish that's somewhat fortunate

indicators.note: somewhat means only part of the following word is used

explanation.surface: A fisherman counts himself lucky with his catch.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit inside forTUNAte; 'that's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A large ocean food fish, often tinned, is a member of the mackerel family.

clue.text: For example, Romeo and Juliet and Dicky gyrated

indicators.note: dicky means unsound or shaky, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's lovers dance about with someone called Dicky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' is the British slang for unsteady, signalling an anagram of GYRATED; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's story of the doomed lovers is a drama ending in death.

clue.text: Land on one's head?

explanation.surface: A country you wear.
explanation.definitionFit: A Central American country, and a straw hat worn on the head.

clue.text: A victory during depression strain evident on pitch

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'A victory during depression strain evident on pitch': A + V in DENT gives the letters, but the definition is lost; 'strain evident on pitch' is copied from 30-across.
annotationWithheld.clue: A victory during depression strain evident on pitch

clue.text: Go through arm

explanation.surface: A soldier searches through his weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: To ransack or rummage through things, and a long gun carried as a weapon.

clue.text: Brilliant directors should be right in the main

parts.note: star as an adjective means brilliant, outstanding
a company's directors form its board

explanation.surface: Outstanding executives ought to be correct about the main business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the main' is the old word for the open sea, so 'right in the main' is the right-hand side of a ship; 'should be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors call the right-hand side of a vessel, facing forward, by this nautical term.

clue.text: Audibly cries out for woollen

indicators.note: audibly means the word for cries out is said aloud

parts.note: bays means howls, cries out

explanation.surface: Someone shouts for a woolly jumper.
explanation.walkthrough: BAYS and BAIZE sound alike; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A green felt-like fabric of wool, used on snooker tables, is a woollen cloth.

clue.text: Go in opposite directions, only not on the ball

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: going in opposite directions means the word is written once forwards and once backwards

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: not means the word on is removed from only

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to a confused player who keeps running both ways without getting near the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: GO forwards then backwards gives GOOG; ONLY without ON leaves LY. A googly is a cricket delivery from a spin bowler that turns the opposite way to what the batter expects.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, a deceptive delivery from a wrist-spinner is a particular kind of bowled ball.

clue.text: Vermin returning in time to wreak havoc

indicators.note: in means the reversed vermin go inside the word for time

parts.note: a date is a point in time

indicators.note: returning means the word for vermin is read backwards

parts.note: mice are vermin

explanation.surface: Rodents come back in time to cause chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' and 'in' are two indicators: the vermin are turned round and set inside the time.
explanation.definitionFit: To destroy a large part of something, literally killing one in ten, is to devastate.

clue.text: False tears broken at last (7)

indicators.note: broken means the letters of the word tears are rearranged

parts.note: Z is the last letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: Fake tears finally break out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' signals the anagram; the alphabet's final letter supplies the closing piece. The stray (7) before (6) is a print slip.
explanation.definitionFit: A German-derived word for an inferior substitute or imitation, not genuine.

clue.text: Playing repetitive roles, strain evident on pitch

indicators.note: on means the second piece follows the first

parts.note: a strain is a type or variety
to cast is to pitch or throw

explanation.surface: An actor always given the same parts shows strain on the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' places pitch after strain in a down-style charade; 'evident' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor always cast in the same sort of part has been pigeonholed by directors.
